qaPairs.question: What is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) and why do we need it?
qaPairs.answer:
RAG is an architecture pattern where you retrieve relevant documents from an external knowledge base and inject them into the LLM's prompt before generating an answer. Instead of relying solely on what the LLM memorized during training, you give it fresh, relevant context at query time. Why we need it: (1) LLMs have a knowledge cutoff — they don't know anything after their training date. (2) LLMs hallucinate — without grounding data, they make things up confidently. (3) Domain-specific knowledge — your company's internal docs, policies, and data aren't in any public LLM. (4) Cheaper than fine-tuning — updating a knowledge base is instant; retraining a model takes days and thousands of dollars.
Example:
Without RAG:
User: 'What is our company refund policy?' LLM: 'Generally, most companies offer 30-day refunds...' (generic, possibly wrong)
With RAG:
Step 1: Search company knowledge base for 'refund policy' Step 2: Retrieve: 'Refund policy: Full refund within 14 days. Store credit after 14 days. No refund after 30 days.' Step 3: Inject into prompt as context Step 4: LLM generates: 'Our refund policy allows full refunds within 14 days, store credit between 14-30 days, and no refunds after 30 days.' Grounded, accurate, company-specific answer.
Interview Tip: Say 'RAG solves three problems: knowledge recency, hallucination grounding, and domain specificity — without the cost of fine-tuning.' This one sentence shows you understand both the WHY and the economics.

qaPairs.question: Explain the complete RAG pipeline step by step.
qaPairs.answer:
The RAG pipeline has two phases — Indexing (offline, done once) and Retrieval + Generation (online, per query). Indexing phase: (1) Load documents (PDFs, web pages, databases). (2) Split documents into chunks (paragraphs, sentences, or fixed-size windows). (3) Generate embeddings for each chunk using an embedding model. (4) Store embeddings + original text in a vector database. Query phase: (1) User asks a question. (2) Generate embedding of the query using the same embedding model. (3) Search vector database for top-K most similar chunks (cosine similarity). (4) Inject retrieved chunks into the LLM prompt as context. (5) LLM generates answer grounded in the retrieved context. (6) Optionally, cite sources.
Example:
Indexing (one-time setup):
500 company PDFs -> split into 15,000 chunks -> embed each chunk using text-embedding-3-small -> store in Pinecone (vector DB) Total time: ~30 minutes, ~$5 embedding cost
Query time (every user question):
User: 'What are the Q3 revenue numbers?' -> Embed query -> search Pinecone -> top 5 chunks returned -> Chunks contain Q3 financial report sections -> LLM reads chunks + generates: 'Q3 revenue was $4.2M, up 18% YoY' Total time: ~2 seconds, ~$0.003 per query
Interview Tip: Draw the pipeline on a whiteboard in two rows — Indexing (offline) and Query (online). Interviewers love visual explanations, and it shows you understand the system architecture.

qaPairs.question: What are the key components of a RAG system and what choices do you make for each?
qaPairs.answer:
Six key components with choices: (1) Document Loader — how you ingest data. Choices: LangChain loaders, Unstructured.io, LlamaIndex. (2) Chunking Strategy — how you split documents. Choices: fixed-size, recursive, semantic, sentence-level. (3) Embedding Model — converts text to vectors. Choices: OpenAI text-embedding-3, Cohere embed-v3, open-source (BGE, E5, Jina). (4) Vector Database — stores and searches embeddings. Choices: Pinecone, Weaviate, ChromaDB, Qdrant, pgvector. (5) Retrieval Strategy — how you search. Choices: dense search, sparse (BM25), hybrid, reranking. (6) LLM Generator — generates the final answer. Choices: GPT-4, Claude, Llama, Mistral. Each choice impacts quality, cost, latency, and accuracy differently.
Example:
Budget-friendly production RAG stack:
Loader: Unstructured.io (handles PDFs, DOCX, HTML) Chunking: Recursive text splitter (512 tokens, 50 token overlap) Embedding: text-embedding-3-small ($0.02/1M tokens) Vector DB: Qdrant (open-source, self-hosted) Retrieval: Hybrid (BM25 + dense) with Cohere reranker LLM: GPT-4o-mini for simple queries, GPT-4 for complex
Premium production RAG stack:
Embedding: text-embedding-3-large Vector DB: Pinecone (managed, serverless) Retrieval: Hybrid + cross-encoder reranking LLM: Claude Opus with streaming
Interview Tip: When asked to design a RAG system, list all 6 components and justify EACH choice. Don't just say 'I would use Pinecone' — say 'I would use Pinecone for managed serverless scaling, but for a cost-sensitive project, Qdrant self-hosted.' Chunking Strategies

qaPairs.question: Why is chunking important and what happens if you get it wrong?
qaPairs.answer:
Chunking is the process of splitting documents into smaller pieces before embedding them. It's arguably the MOST important step in RAG because it directly determines what gets retrieved. If chunks are too large: (1) Each chunk contains mixed topics, diluting the embedding's meaning. (2) You waste context window tokens on irrelevant text. (3) Retrieval precision drops. If chunks are too small: (1) Context is fragmented — the answer spans multiple chunks but only one gets retrieved. (2) Loss of surrounding context makes chunks meaningless. (3) More chunks = higher storage and search costs. The sweet spot depends on your content type, but typically 256-1024 tokens with 10-20% overlap.
Example:
Document: A 5-page refund policy document.
Too large (entire document as 1 chunk):
User asks about 'return window' -> retrieves ALL 5 pages LLM gets overwhelmed with irrelevant shipping, warranty info Answer quality: Poor (lost in the noise)
Too small (every sentence as 1 chunk):
Chunk: 'Returns must be made within 14 days.' Misses: '...from the date of delivery, with original packaging.' Answer quality: Incomplete
Just right (paragraph-level, ~300 tokens):
Chunk: 'Returns must be made within 14 days from the date of delivery, with original packaging. Items must be unused and in resalable condition. Refund will be processed within 5-7 business days.' Answer quality: Complete and accurate
Interview Tip: Say 'Chunking is where most RAG systems fail. I always experiment with 3-4 chunk sizes and evaluate retrieval quality before finalizing.' This shows you don't just set defaults — you optimize.

qaPairs.question: What are the different chunking methods and when do you use each?
qaPairs.answer:
Five main approaches: (1) Fixed-size chunking — split every N tokens/characters. Simple but can break sentences mid-thought. Use for: uniform documents like logs. (2) Recursive text splitting — split by paragraphs first, then sentences, then characters as fallback. Most popular default. Use for: general documents. (3) Sentence-level splitting — each chunk is one or more complete sentences. Preserves grammatical meaning. Use for: FAQs, Q&A pairs. (4) Semantic chunking — uses embeddings to find natural topic boundaries. Groups sentences with similar meaning together. Use for: long documents with multiple topics. (5) Document-structure-aware — uses headings, sections, tables as chunk boundaries. Respects document layout. Use for: structured docs like legal contracts, technical manuals, research papers.
Example:
Same document, different strategies:
Document: 'Machine Learning Overview' (10 pages) Fixed (512 tokens): 20 chunks, some split mid-sentence Recursive: 18 chunks, clean paragraph boundaries Semantic: 12 chunks, each covering one concept Structure-aware: 8 chunks (Intro, Types of ML, Supervised, Unsupervised, DL, Applications, Challenges, Conclusion)
Retrieval test with query 'What is supervised learning?':
Fixed: Retrieved chunk has half supervised + half unsupervised (confused) Recursive: Retrieved chunk has full supervised section (good) Semantic: Retrieved chunk has supervised + relevant examples (best) Structure-aware: Retrieved exact 'Supervised Learning' section (best)
Interview Tip: Mention 'semantic chunking' proactively. Most candidates only know fixed-size. Saying 'I use semantic chunking with embedding similarity to find natural topic boundaries' puts you ahead of 90% of candidates.

qaPairs.question: What is chunk overlap and why is it critical?
qaPairs.answer:
Chunk overlap means consecutive chunks share some tokens at their boundaries. If chunk 1 ends at position 500 and chunk 2 starts at position 450, there's a 50-token overlap. Why it matters: Information often spans chunk boundaries. Without overlap, a sentence split across two chunks loses its meaning in both. With overlap, the critical boundary content appears in BOTH chunks, so retrieval can find it regardless of which chunk it searches. Typical overlap: 10-20% of chunk size. If chunk size is 512 tokens, use 50-100 token overlap. Too much overlap = redundancy and storage waste. Too little = information loss at boundaries.
Example:
Document text:
'...The model achieved 94% accuracy on the test set. However, the precision for class B was only 67%. This indicates significant class imbalance issues...'
Without overlap (chunk boundary after 'test set.'):
Chunk 1: '...The model achieved 94% accuracy on the test set.' Chunk 2: 'However, the precision for class B was only 67%. This indicates...' Query: 'What was the model accuracy?' -> Retrieves Chunk 1 but misses the precision problem
With 50-token overlap:
Chunk 1: '...The model achieved 94% accuracy on the test set. However, the precision for class B was only 67%.' Chunk 2: 'However, the precision for class B was only 67%. This indicates significant class imbalance issues...' Query: 'What was the model accuracy?' -> Retrieves Chunk 1 with COMPLETE context including the precision caveat
Interview Tip: Say 'I always use 10-20% overlap to prevent information loss at chunk boundaries.' Simple, practical, shows you've built real RAG systems. Embeddings & Vector Databases
